questions.q: What does this lesson identify as the single most common, most serious code review finding?
options: A SOQL query or DML statement sitting inside a for loop
A missing code comment
A class declared without an access modifier
A variable named with camelCase instead of PascalCase
questions.explain: A query or DML statement inside a loop is called out as the single most common, most serious finding, since it scales badly and can breach governor limits at real-world volume.

questions.q: What should a reviewer check first when reviewing an unfamiliar trigger handler, per this lesson?
options: Whether the code uses tabs or spaces for indentation
Whether the trigger has a comment at the top explaining its author
Whether the handler correctly assumes it could receive up to 200 records, rather than being written as if it only ever processes one
Whether the trigger fires on the Account object specifically
questions.explain: This lesson states that confirming the handler correctly handles a full batch of records, rather than assuming a single record, is the foundational check — if that assumption is wrong, nearly everything else about the review is invalidated.

questions.q: Which of these is described as a hard rule with no legitimate exception, rather than a judgment call?
options: Whether a given piece of automation needs full Selector/Service layering
Whether to use with sharing or without sharing for a specific class
Whether to name a variable acctList or accounts
A SOQL query placed inside a for loop
questions.explain: A SOQL query inside a loop is explicitly called a hard rule with no legitimate exception, unlike layering decisions or sharing-keyword choices, which the lesson treats as reasonable judgment calls.

questions.q: Why is an empty `catch (Exception e) {}` block flagged as a code review concern?
options: Because Apex does not allow empty catch blocks to compile
Because it silently swallows a real problem instead of handling or logging it deliberately
Because it is slower than not using try/catch at all
Because it only works with DmlException, not other exception types
questions.explain: An empty catch block hides exceptions instead of handling them deliberately, which is exactly the kind of silent failure a code reviewer should catch and question.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say finding more than one trigger on the same object and event is a reviewable finding?
options: Execution order across multiple triggers on the same object and event isn't guaranteed, which Lesson 22 covers as a reason to keep one trigger per object
Salesforce doesn't technically allow more than one trigger per object
Multiple triggers always cause a compile error
It has no real consequence; it's purely a style preference
questions.explain: Per Lesson 22, having more than one trigger on the same object and event makes execution order unpredictable, which is why a reviewer should flag it as a real concern, not just a style nitpick.
